title: Answering well: structure, scope & examples
blurb: A simple structure for every answer, the language that keeps you within scope, how to bring in reflection, and what to do when you're unsure.
question: The assessor asks: "How do you protect patient confidentiality?" One learner says, "I keep everything confidential and follow GDPR." Another tells a short story about a real phone call, explains why she acted as she did and what she changed afterwards. Why is the second answer so much stronger, and how can you answer like that every time?

teach.body: NEBDN hasn't published the questions or a marking grid, but it has said what the discussion is based on: the nine duties, your workplace activities and the GDC Scope of Practice. So a strong answer gives a real example, says clearly what YOU did, explains why (the GDC standard, guidance or law behind it), stays inside your scope, and shows what you learned. That pattern works for almost any question on any duty.

steps.label: Situation
steps.sub: A real example, briefly and anonymously

steps.label: Action
steps.sub: What I did, and who made any clinical decision

steps.label: Why
steps.sub: The GDC standard, guidance or law behind it

steps.label: Reflection
steps.sub: What I learned and what I now do differently

teach.caption: Keep the Action inside your scope. If the dentist diagnosed or planned, say so, then describe your part.

teach.body: "Last month a man phoned asking if his wife had been in that morning. I didn't confirm she was a patient. I offered to take a message and let the dentist know. GDC principle 4 says we must protect patients' information, and under UK GDPR we can't share it without consent or a lawful reason. Afterwards I realised I'd felt awkward saying no, so I asked my manager for a standard reply, and now I handle those calls confidently."

teach.h: Language that keeps you within scope
teach.body: Dental nurses don't diagnose or plan treatment, so say: "the dentist diagnosed…", "as prescribed by the dentist…", "I recorded…", "I prepared…", "I told the dentist…". Avoid: "I diagnosed", "I decided the treatment", or "I told the patient it was nothing". For additional skills, make the condition clear, for example "once I'm trained, competent and indemnified". Being precise about who does what is itself evidence of duty 5 and personal accountability.

The reflection step is where you show insight and that you keep developing (duty 8). Reflective models help you think it through beforehand. Kolb's cycle is simple to use: you have an experience, reflect on it, draw a conclusion, then try out the new approach, which becomes your next experience. Ending an answer with "so now I…" shows the cycle working in real life.

teach.caption: Experience it, reflect on it, work out what it means, try the new approach. Gibbs' cycle and "What? So what? Now what?" work just as well.

teach.h: Using the reading time and the discussion
items: NEBDN hasn't said what the reading material contains, so read whatever you're given carefully and calmly.
Note which duties it seems to touch, and jot a keyword for an example you could use.
In the discussion, listen to the whole question before answering.
It's fine to pause, or to ask the assessor to repeat or clarify a question.
Answer with one clear example rather than a long list of everything you know.

root.label: A question you can't fully answer

children.label: Be honest
children.sub: Say how you'd find out: dentist, policy, guidance

teach.caption: Knowing your limits and seeking advice is part of the dental nurse standard. Guessing or bluffing is the riskier choice.

teach.text: Saying "we" all the time hides your role. The duties are about what YOU do. Use "I" for your actions, name who made clinical decisions, and keep examples real: invented stories are hard to explain under follow-up questions.

items: Use real, anonymous examples from your own workplace and portfolio.
Name the GDC standard, guidance or law that explains why you acted.
Scope language: the dentist diagnoses and plans; you record, prepare, support and report.
If unsure, be honest and explain how you'd find out; that shows insight.

summary: You can now structure any answer as Situation, Action, Why and Reflection, use language that stays inside the dental nurse's scope, link your actions to GDC standards, bring in reflection with a model such as Kolb's, and handle questions you're unsure about with honesty and insight.

A.q: The assessor asks, "How do you prepare the surgery for an extraction?" Which opening is strongest?
options: "Extractions need lots of instruments, so it depends really."
"Last week I set up for an extraction on a patient on warfarin…"
"We always just do exactly what the dentist tells us to do there."
"The textbook lists forceps, elevators and gauze for this."
A.why: Starting with a real, specific example from your own workplace sets up a strong answer you can then explain and reflect on.

whyNot.0: This is vague and gives the assessor nothing specific.
whyNot.2: "We" hides your role, and it suggests you don't understand why.
whyNot.3: Textbook lists show knowledge, not what you actually do at work.

A.q: Which statement keeps a clinical example within the dental nurse's scope?
options: "I could see the abscess, so I set up for an extraction."
"I told the patient the tooth would definitely need to come out."
"I chose the extraction over a root filling for her."
"The dentist diagnosed an abscess; I prepared and assisted."
A.why: It makes clear the dentist diagnosed and planned, and describes the nurse's supporting role.

whyNot.0: This implies you diagnosed the abscess and decided the treatment.
whyNot.1: Telling a patient their treatment is giving a diagnosis and plan.
whyNot.2: Choosing treatment is treatment planning, which dental nurses don't do.

A.q: In Kolb's learning cycle, which stage involves trying out the new approach in practice?
options: Concrete experience
Reflective observation
Active experimentation
Abstract conceptualisation
A.why: Active experimentation is where you put what you've learned into practice, which creates a new experience.

whyNot.0: Concrete experience is the event itself.
whyNot.1: Reflective observation is looking back on the experience.
whyNot.3: Abstract conceptualisation is drawing conclusions about what it means.

B.q: The assessor asks something you genuinely don't know. What is the best response?
options: Say you're unsure and explain how you'd find out
Guess confidently so that you don't look unprepared
Change the subject to a duty you know better
Say it isn't relevant to dental nurses
B.why: Being honest and explaining how you'd seek advice shows insight into your limits, which is part of safe practice.

whyNot.1: Bluffing risks giving unsafe or wrong information.
whyNot.2: Avoiding the question doesn't answer it and may look evasive.
whyNot.3: Dismissing a question without thought isn't professional.

B.q: Why should you link your examples to a GDC standard or guidance?
options: It makes the answer sound longer and more formal
It shows you understand why you acted that way
It is the only part of the answer that matters
It lets you avoid giving a real example
B.why: Explaining the standard or guidance behind an action shows professional understanding and accountability, not just habit.

whyNot.0: Length and formality aren't the point; understanding is.
whyNot.2: The example, your role and your reflection matter too.
whyNot.3: Standards support real examples; they don't replace them.

B.q: Which answer best shows personal accountability?
options: "We all keep an eye on the emergency drugs kit between us."
"Someone usually checks the emergency drugs on Monday mornings."
"The practice manager is the one responsible for the drugs kit."
"I saw a drug was out of date, removed it and told my manager."
B.why: It shows you personally noticed a risk, acted and reported it, which is personal accountability in action.

whyNot.0: "We all" doesn't show what you did.
whyNot.1: This is vague and suggests no one takes clear responsibility.
whyNot.2: This passes responsibility to someone else.

C.q: NEBDN hasn't said what the reading material contains. How is the 10 minutes of reading time best used?
options: Rest your eyes and save your energy for the discussion itself
Write a full script to read out word for word
Read carefully and note duties and examples it suggests
Search online for model answers that match the material
C.why: Reading carefully and noting which duties and examples come to mind prepares you to answer, whatever the material is.

whyNot.0: Not reading wastes the time you've been given.
whyNot.1: Reading a script sounds rehearsed and stops it being a discussion.
whyNot.3: Looking up answers during an assessment would be malpractice.

C.q: Which order follows the answer structure taught in this lesson?
options: Why, Reflection, Situation, Action
Situation, Action, Why, Reflection
Action, Situation, Reflection, Why
Reflection, Why, Action, Situation
C.why: Set the scene, say what you did, explain why, then reflect on what you learned and changed.

whyNot.0: Starting with why, before the example, is hard to follow.
whyNot.2: The situation should come before the action.
whyNot.3: Reflection comes last, after the story and the reasons.

C.q: You aren't certified to take radiographs, and the assessor asks about radiography. What is the best answer?
options: Explain who takes them, then describe your own part
Describe taking radiographs as if you had done it yourself
Say radiography has nothing to do with nurses
Refuse to answer as it's outside your scope
C.why: Explaining that taking radiographs needs certification, then describing what you do (such as processing images and supporting the patient), shows accurate scope awareness.

whyNot.1: Claiming tasks you haven't done is dishonest and outside your scope.
whyNot.2: Processing and managing radiographs is part of routine dental nurse work.
whyNot.3: You can still discuss your supporting role and the safety rules you follow.

reteach.title: Tell it like a good story
reteach.question: Think of the best story a friend has told you. Why did it stick?

blocks.body: Good stories have a setting, something that happens, a reason it matters and an ending where someone has changed. Your answers work the same way. The setting is the situation. What happens is what you did. The reason is the standard or guidance behind it. The ending is your reflection: what you learned and now do differently. Without an ending, a story just stops, and so does an answer.

blocks.text: The hero of your story is you, but the dentist still makes the clinical decisions. Be the main character without taking the dentist's role.

explain.body: Situation (a real example), Action (what I did), Why (the standard, guidance or law), Reflection (what I learned and changed).

test.q: Which part of the answer structure names the GDC standard behind your action?
options: Situation
Reflection
Action
Why
test.why: The "Why" step explains the standard, guidance or law that justifies what you did.

whyNot.1: Reflection covers what you learned and changed.

explain.body: Say what the dentist decided, then what you did. Never claim to diagnose, plan treatment or reassure a patient about a diagnosis.

test.q: Which phrase would raise a scope concern in your discussion?
options: "I recorded the charting the dentist dictated."
"I told the dentist about the patient's new tablets."
"I reassured the patient her lump was nothing."
"I prepared the surgery as the dentist prescribed."
test.why: Telling a patient a lump is nothing is making a diagnosis, which is outside a dental nurse's scope and could delay referral.

whyNot.0: Recording dictated charting is within scope.
whyNot.1: Reporting a change to the dentist is exactly right.
whyNot.3: Preparing as prescribed is within scope.

explain.body: Concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation. End your answer with what you now do differently.

test.q: Which stage of Kolb's cycle is "working out what the experience means and what principle it shows"?
options: Abstract conceptualisation
Concrete experience
Active experimentation
Reflective observation
test.why: Abstract conceptualisation is where you draw conclusions and form ideas from your reflection.

whyNot.1: Concrete experience is the event itself.
whyNot.2: Active experimentation is trying the new approach.
whyNot.3: Reflective observation is looking back on what happened.

explain.body: Be honest and explain how you'd find out. If a task is outside your scope, say who does it and describe your supporting part.

test.q: Why is saying "I'm not sure, but I'd check the practice policy and ask the dentist" a good answer?
options: It avoids having to answer at all
It shows insight into your limits
It moves the blame onto the dentist
It makes the question count less
test.why: Recognising your limits and seeking advice shows insight, which is part of safe, accountable practice.

whyNot.0: You are still answering, by explaining how you'd act safely.
whyNot.3: NEBDN hasn't published how answers are weighted, and this doesn't change it.
